title: On Struggle:
summary: Thoughts on AI and how one of the most important parts of learning became optional.

sections.heading: Delegation
sections.body:
I think one of my strongest opinions on learning and AI use is to absolutely delegate almost (key word here) everything you are uninterested in learning to AI. Its probably more important to distinguish between coding with the intention of building a product and coding with the intention of learning.

In both cases you'd obviously want to know what whatever you're running does and why. But if I'm learning about data analytics and a clean visual is in no way associated with (but it can be!) the analysis im doing I'm perfectly fine having a nice looking AI gen'd frontend.

sections.heading: The Problem of Dopamine
sections.body:
Theres also the aspect of "human purity" that also presents an issue for learning while building. It's been the case in the past that you'd get an amazing rewarding feeling for struggling through something on your own and building but now there's essentially a button that does it for you, and possibly better. At times it also feels like theres some credit being taken away by asking models for help, especially when they tend to respond with inplementation supplemented assistance.

Whats more is theres always this urge to give in and immediately get the solution or the completed version for a lesser feeling of acomplishment.

Yes, the task is done, but theres no struggle or head banging on the wall.

sections.heading: A Dystopian Token Slave
sections.body: Kinda related kinda not, but a friend of mine named Dennis sent the image below from Twitter earlier this year and it really made me think about AI use and how heavily delegating things I care about learning or understanding deeply will end up eroding my ability as an engineer.

That is to say, I don't want to end up as a token slave, dependent on AI to do everything. I think the biggest issue is we slowly move from outsourcing info gathering to outsourcing reasoning.

`We gradually lose the ability to recognize what we don't understand.`

sections.heading: Slop and Sytems
sections.body:
I think this whole conversation ties a bit into why I want to become more well versed in the systems programming space. 

I think when there are a lot of abstractions to work with, it becomes easier to meaningfully talk about, work on, or understand things with imprecision.

This is true of systems programming as well but its very prevalent in web app development and adjacent spaces. It seems to me however, that in lower-level environments, you often may need to cash out abstractions into something concrete. What memory is being touched? What runtimes are being used? How will performance change if multiple threads are involved?

I'm not interested in this space because it is somehow AI-immune. It's that it makes me frequently confront the boundary of what I can describe vs what I actually understand. 

I hope that by actively learning more about software in such a way where my gaps in knowledge are readily apparent, and continuing to bang my head on stuff I care about, I can become a great engineer in the AI landscape.
